newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Goldstone says U.N. war crimes tribunal could fail.
newsitem.headline: Goldstone says U.N. war crimes tribunal could fail.

text.p: The U.N. criminal tribunal for ex-Yugoslavia could fail because the international community lacks the will to arrest those indicted for war crimes, its outgoing chief prosecutor Richard Goldstone said on Wednesday.

In a speech delivered in the Dutch city of Utrecht, Goldstone said it was frustrating and disappointing that only seven of the 75 suspects indicted by the tribunal had been arrested and transferred to its detention centre in The Hague.

"The international community itself set up the tribunal. The warrants of arrest we issue are issued in the name of the international community...and it's the international community's political will that has wanted," he said.

"If in fact the tribunal fails, as it could and probably will if this continues long enough, because if we're not allowed to do the job we were created to do, then what's the point in keeping the tribunal going?" he said.

Those indicted, but not yet arrested, include deposed Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic, both of whom have been charged with genocide for the massacre of Moslems at Srebrenica in July 1995.

Goldstone's speech contrasted with mildly optimistic comments made to journalists in The Hague earlier on Wednesday in which he had said the recent Bosnian elections could speed up the arrest of indicted war crimes suspects.

"To be optimistic would be overstating it, but I think there are good prospects of an arrest taking place," Goldstone said, referring to Karadzic, the wartime Bosnian Serb leader, and Mladic, his military commander.
Following the elections, Bosnia's own police force was in a better position to arrest "expendable ex-politicians", he said.
Goldstone is due to hand over his post to Canadian judge Louise Arbour at the end of this month and return to his native South Africa to take up a seat on its constitutional court.

Created by the U.N. Security Council in May 1993, the Yugoslavia tribunal was the first international body for the prosecution of war crimes since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials held in the aftermath of World War Two.
A similar U.N. tribunal was later set up to try those responsible for the genocide in Rwanda.
